questions.prompt: In C++23, which of these `static_assert`s fails?
questions.explanation: A `static_assert` on a false condition makes the program ill-formed, so line C fails to compile. A view must be cheap to copy if it is copyable, and copying a `std::vector` copies every element, so `enable_view<std::vector<int>>` is `false`. The standard specializes `enable_view` for `basic_string_view` and `span`, and `ref_view` derives from `view_interface`, which opts it in. `ref_view` is a view because it only stores a pointer to the vector.

Building a view evaluates nothing: `r` stores a `ref_view` of `v` and the lambda, so `calls` is still 0. `r[2]` advances the iterator by 2, which does not call the function, and then dereferences once, so exactly one call computes `3 * 3`. The tempting `4` answers assume the adaptor transforms the whole vector up front, which is how an eager `std::transform` into a new container behaves.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what is the type of `views::all(std::vector<int>{1, 2})`?
options: It is ill-formed: an rvalue container cannot be turned into a view
questions.explanation: `views::all` copies an argument that is already a view, wraps an lvalue in `ref_view`, and moves any other rvalue range into an `owning_view`. A `ref_view` of a temporary would dangle immediately, which is why it is not chosen. The ill-formed answer describes C++20 as originally published; P2415R2 added `owning_view` and was applied to C++20 as a defect report.

The filter checks each element by dereferencing the transform iterator, which costs four calls, and the loop dereferences each of the two kept elements again, for six. On the second loop, `filter_view::begin()` returns the iterator it cached the first time, so the search that examined `1` and `2` is skipped; the remaining calls are `2` dereferenced in the loop, `3` and `4` checked, and `4` dereferenced, which is four. `6 6` is the answer if you forget the cache.

options: Yes: a `const&` parameter binds to the temporary view
Ill-formed: a view cannot bind to a reference parameter
Undefined behavior: the view is a temporary
questions.explanation: `filter_view::begin()` must cache the first matching iterator to meet the amortized constant-time requirement of `range`, so it is a non-`const` member and `const filter_view` does not model `range`. The range-based `for` on `const auto&` therefore finds no usable `begin`. The binding itself is fine, and the temporary lives until the end of the full-expression, so the other answers are wrong; take views by value or by `auto&&`.

options: It returns 3, counting matches in linear time
It returns 4, the size of the underlying vector
Undefined behavior, because `size` was called before iterating
The program is ill-formed: `filter_view` is not a `sized_range`
questions.explanation: `ranges::size` only works when the size is available in amortized constant time: through a `size()` member or free function, or by subtracting a sized sentinel from the iterator. `filter_view` has neither, because its size depends on how many elements pass the predicate, so the call does not compile. Use `std::ranges::distance(f)`, which is allowed to walk the range and returns 3 here.

questions.prompt: What does the standard say about this loop?
options: It is ill-formed: `filter_view` iterators are read-only
It is undefined behavior, because the modified elements no longer satisfy the predicate
It is well-defined, but iterating `evens` again visits no elements
questions.explanation: [range.filter.iterator] permits modifying the element a `filter_view` iterator denotes, but says the behavior is undefined if the new value does not satisfy the predicate. Adding 1 to an even number makes it odd, so the loop breaks the view's invariant. The iterators do yield `int&`, so the code compiles, and observing `1 3 3 5` on a real implementation does not make it defined. Writing a value that stays even would be fine.

questions.prompt: Which of these is **not** a requirement of the `std::ranges::view` concept in C++23?
questions.explanation: `view<T>` is `range<T> && movable<T> && enable_view<T>`, with semantic requirements that move construction is constant time and that copies and destruction are cheap. C++20 as published also required `default_initializable`, but P2325R3 removed it and was applied to C++20 as a defect report, so a view such as `ref_view` need not have a default constructor. The other three options are all still required.
